studyPath.intro: A route through Week 3 for someone meeting discounting for the first time. All four topics in my Notion note are written now, so this is a long week — twenty-five sections that build from one year’s cash flow to a verdict on four competing appraisal measures — and a full pass runs to a bit over three hours.

steps.label: Read sections 01 to 13 first
steps.detail: Concept of present value carries the whole week — every later topic assumes you can restate a future cash flow in today’s terms. Slow right down at sections 03 and 04: the $2000 excess is value in future-dollar terms and the $1818 is value created today, and the week only works if those stay two different numbers in your head. Then read Investment Appraisal, 06 to 13, straight through, and finish at the 7% / 10% / 14% table where the preferred project changes twice.

steps.label: Then 14 to 25, the two topics that follow
steps.detail: Stay on the same tab and use the topic chips above the contents list — Internal rate of return, then Problems with common approaches — so you read one argument at a time rather than twenty-five sections at once. The week is long enough that every section starts collapsed, so open them as you go, or hit Expand all. Read 14 to 18 for what IRR is and where it disagrees with NPV, then 19 to 25, which is the same three-criteria test applied to payback, average accounting ROA and IRR in turn. Section 23 is the heaviest: reinvestment assumption and scale problem in one block.

steps.label: Fix the vocabulary that overlaps
steps.detail: Sixty-six terms, and the ones worth filtering for are the near-synonyms: cost of capital, discount rate, required return and hurdle rate all name the same quantity from different angles, and the notes write it as Hurdle Rate / WACC / cost of capital in one breath. Several terms appear more than once with different source tags — Net Present Value under three topics, Internal Rate of Return under two — and the duplicates are not redundant, because each one records what that topic says about it. While you are here, the Acronyms tab is a short detour: CF0, CFn and WACC are used in the notes without ever being written out, so that tab supplies the standard expansions and says which ones it had to.

steps.label: Audit what the notes actually state
steps.detail: Do this before you try to revise from them, so you know where the gaps are. Several relationships this week discusses are absent by design: the symbolic present-value formula, its worked example, the average return on assets calculation and the two Excel NPV() illustrations all sat in images that were never published, and nothing has been reconstructed in their place. The average-return line is reproduced exactly as I typed it, truncation and all — do not read it as a finished figure, and do not go looking for the ROA calculation anywhere on this page, because the Problems topic states in words that it is not here.

steps.label: Drill the ninety-six cards until automatic
steps.detail: Too many for one sitting — split them, and shuffle before the second pass, because the deck follows page order and you will otherwise be recalling position rather than content. Two runs of cards carry most of the week’s discriminating power: the 7% / 10% / 14% cards, where you should be able to say which project wins at each rate and why before you flip, and the three standalone-IRR cards, where above, equal to and below the hurdle rate give three different verdicts.

steps.label: Test the confusions that bite
steps.detail: Twenty-six questions, weighted toward present value early in the week and toward the appraisal measures at the end. Read the feedback on the options you did not pick as well as the one you did — the distractors are built from the specific mix-ups this week invites: future surplus against value created today, reported loss against cash generated, percentage return against dollar value created, and the highest IRR against the highest NPV.

steps.label: Reason through the seven scenarios
steps.detail: These are where the week stops being arithmetic and becomes a judgement about someone else’s paper. Take the hints one at a time rather than opening all three, and leave the three-measures, higher-IRR and bigger-percentage scenarios until last, since each assumes you already accept that a ranking is a joint property of the cash flows and the rate applied to them. Then close the laptop and talk the one-year example through out loud, from the $100,000 of capital to the $1818 of value created, without looking.

studyPath.close: The week has landed when I can explain, without notes, why a project reporting an accounting loss may still be the one creating value, why two projects that repay at the same speed are not the same investment, and why the higher percentage return is not automatically the better project.

quizIntro: Twenty-six questions across the week’s four topics: discounting and net present value, profit against cash flow and the hurdle rate, the internal rate of return and where it disagrees with NPV, and what payback, average accounting ROA and a percentage return each leave out. The feedback opens straight away on every option rather than only the right one, so a wrong pick tells me which confusion I fell into.
applyIntro: Seven situations to reason through with this week’s tools rather than questions with a single line answer. Each gives three hints that unfold one at a time, so I can take only as much help as I need, and the walkthrough that follows uses nothing beyond what this page states — including where the notes leave a definition or a calculation unpublished, and where the figure I typed is truncated.

quiz.q: What does present value (PV) convert a future cash flow into?
quiz.hint: The week’s opening move is about which point in time the number is expressed at.

options.t: The nominal amount of capital originally committed to obtain it.
options.note: That is the initial outlay, which NPV subtracts. Present value is what the future cash flow itself is worth today.

options.t: Its value at the end of the investment’s life, once the required return has accrued.
options.note: That runs the arithmetic the other way — the $100,000 growing to $110,000 is a future-dollar figure. Present value moves a future amount back to today.

options.t: Its equivalent value today.
options.note: The page’s first line: present value converts a future cash flow into its equivalent value today.

options.t: The accounting profit the investment will report in the year the cash arrives.
options.note: This is the profit-versus-cash-flow confusion the week spends a whole section on. Present value is about timing, not about how earnings are reported.

quiz.q: According to the week, why is a dollar promised in a year worth less than a dollar held now?
quiz.hint: The page names one mechanism, and it is the same thing it calls r.

options.t: Because capital carries a required return — a cost of capital.
options.note: Exactly the reason the page gives: a future dollar is worth less because capital has a required return, and the discount rate represents the return required for committing capital to the investment.

options.t: Because prices rise over the year, so the same dollar buys less.
options.note: Inflation is not the mechanism this page names. It attributes the whole discount to the return capital requires.

options.t: Because depreciation reduces the asset’s book value over the year.
options.note: Depreciation belongs to the profit-versus-cash-flow section and is an accounting charge, not the reason future cash is discounted.

options.t: Because the cash flow may not arrive at all, so it is written down for that chance.
options.note: Risk appears on this page as what sets the hurdle rate, not as a separate write-down. The discount rate is the required return, and risk raises or lowers that rate.

quiz.q: What happens to a present value when a higher discount rate is applied, and why?
quiz.hint: The page states the direction as a rule and then gives the reason in the same sentence.

options.t: It rises, because a larger rate compounds the cash flow further before it is received.
options.note: Compounding pushes value forward; discounting pulls it back. The page states the opposite direction — a higher rate gives a lower present value.

options.t: It is unchanged, because the rate affects only how projects are ranked against each other.
options.note: The rate changes the number itself, not just the ranking. The week later adds that rankings can move too, but that is a separate point.

options.t: It is unchanged for a one-year cash flow and falls only for cash flows further out.
options.note: The page applies the rule to the one-year case it works through. Distance changes how heavily a flow is discounted, not whether it is discounted.

options.t: It falls, because investors require greater compensation for supplying capital.
options.note: The page states it as a rule: higher discount rate → lower present value, because investors require greater compensation for supplying capital.

quiz.q: $100,000 of capital costs 10%, so it must grow to $110,000 after one year; the investment instead generates $112,000. How does the week describe the $2000 difference?
quiz.hint: The week is emphatic that this figure and the value the investment creates are not the same amount.

options.t: As the value the investment creates today.
options.note: This is the confusion the section exists to prevent. The value created today is the discounted figure, $1818, not the $2000.

options.t: As value created in future-dollar terms, which must itself be discounted.
options.note: The page calls the $2000 excess value created in future-dollar terms, then discounts it — $2000/1.10 = $1818 — because the future surplus and today’s value creation are not the same amount.

options.t: As the accounting profit the investment reports for the year.
options.note: The comparison here is cash against the return capital requires, not an earnings figure. Profit enters the week later, in the depreciation section.

options.t: As the present value of the future cash flow.
options.note: The present value of the future cash flow in this example is $101,818. The $2000 is only the amount by which the cash generated exceeds what the capital had to earn.

quiz.q: The worked example gives NPV = $101818 - $100000 = $1818. What is the $101818?
quiz.hint: Two of the three figures in that line already appear earlier in the week under different names.

options.t: The cash the investment generates in one year.
options.note: That is the $112,000, stated in future dollars. It has to be expressed in today’s terms before it can sit alongside the outlay.

options.t: The capital required today to obtain the investment.
options.note: That is the $100000 being subtracted — the initial outlay, not the present value.

options.t: The present value of the future cash flow, expressed in today’s terms.
options.note: It is the future $112,000 discounted at a 10% cost of capital. The page is explicit that the outlay is not compared directly with the nominal future cash flow.

options.t: The amount the capital must grow to over the year to satisfy its required return.
options.note: That benchmark is $110,000. It is what the investment must beat, not the present value of what it delivers.

quiz.q: Two mutually exclusive projects deliver the same strategic or service outcome. What does the week say appraisal is actually being asked?
quiz.hint: Note what the page says appraisal is not asked, immediately before it says what it is asked.

options.t: Which project looks best when it is examined on its own.
options.note: The page rules this out in so many words: appraisal is not asked which project looks best on its own.

options.t: Which project reports the highest accounting profit over its life.
options.note: The page warns that the greatest-value project is not necessarily the one reporting the highest accounting profit — that is the trap, not the test.

options.t: Whether both projects can be accommodated within the same capital budget.
options.note: Mutually exclusive means selecting one is rejecting the other, so accommodating both is not on the table.

options.t: Which of them creates the greatest economic value.
options.note: That is the question the page sets, and it is why it then separates three candidate measures: total accounting profit, average return on assets, and NPV.

quiz.q: Why does the week add depreciation back to profit to arrive at cash flow?
quiz.hint: Ask what money actually left the business when the charge was recorded.

options.t: Because depreciation is an accounting expense but not a current cash outflow, so adding it back recovers the cash the project actually generated.
options.note: The page’s reasoning exactly: profit is reported after a charge that no money left the business to pay, hence Cash Flow = Profit + Depreciation.

options.t: Because depreciation is a cash cost that the profit figure leaves out entirely.
options.note: It is the reverse on both counts — depreciation is already deducted in arriving at profit, and it is not a cash cost.

options.t: Because depreciation must be discounted before the outlay can be subtracted from it.
options.note: This mixes two separate steps. Adding depreciation back is about getting to cash; discounting is what happens to the cash afterwards.

options.t: Because tax relief on depreciation increases the cash the project generates.
options.note: The page states the relationship with taxes excluded, so tax effects are outside what it claims here.

quiz.q: A project reports an accounting loss for the year. On this week’s reasoning, what can still be true of it?
quiz.hint: The relationship between profit and cash flow works in both directions, not only upward.

options.t: Nothing useful — a reported loss means the project consumed cash over the year.
options.note: The whole point of the section is that the two can diverge. A loss is a statement about earnings, not about cash.

options.t: It can still be generating positive cash flow, because depreciation is charged against profit without money leaving the business.
options.note: The page says this directly, and adds that for investment valuation the relevant measure is the cash generated, because value depends on the cash available to investors.

options.t: Its NPV must also be negative, because NPV is built from reported earnings.
options.note: NPV evaluates projects using their actual cash-flow pattern rather than accounting profit, so a reported loss does not settle it.

options.t: Its average return on assets must be positive to offset the loss.
options.note: Average ROA is one of the three candidate measures, not a counterweight that has to balance a reported loss.

quiz.q: Which three drivers of value does the week say accounting profit does not directly incorporate?
quiz.hint: The page sets them out as a single line, and it is the reason profit can mislead a ranking.

options.t: Revenue, cost and depreciation.
options.note: These are inputs to the profit figure itself, so profit could hardly fail to incorporate them. The drivers the page names sit outside the earnings calculation.

options.t: Profit, depreciation and tax.
options.note: Depreciation and tax appear in the week only in the step from profit to cash flow, and the page explicitly excludes taxes from that relationship.

options.t: Capital, required return and initial outlay.
options.note: These belong to the present-value section. They are how value is measured, not the drivers profit misses.

options.t: Cash flow, timing of cash flow and risk.
options.note: The page states them as a line and draws the consequence: ranking investments purely by total profit can produce ‘a different decisions’ from ranking them by economic value. The same three return later as the criteria every appraisal method is tested against.

quiz.q: What limitation does the week attach to average return on assets as an appraisal measure?
quiz.hint: Look at what family of measure the page says it belongs to, and work forward from there.

options.t: It cannot be applied to an asset that is fully depreciated over its life.
options.note: The fully depreciated case is precisely the illustration the notes work through, so this is not the limitation being raised.

options.t: It needs a hurdle rate, and the week says justifying that rate is difficult.
options.note: The hurdle-rate problem attaches to NPV, which depends on the required rate of return applied to the cash flows. Average ROA is an accounting measure and does not use one.

options.t: It remains an accounting-based measure, so it does not fully incorporate cash-flow timing or risk.
options.note: The page calls it an accounting-based return measure — spelt ‘mesaure’ in the notes — and says it does not fully incorporate cash flow timing or risk. The Problems with common approaches topic later takes the same measure apart on three separate grounds.

options.t: It always favours whichever project delivers its cash earlier.
options.note: The page says the opposite risk: it can favour a project with higher accounting profits even where another project generates cash earlier.

quiz.q: What rule does the week give for choosing between mutually exclusive projects?
quiz.hint: The rule comes with two conditions attached, and the conditions are the interesting part.

options.t: Prefer the project with the highest positive NPV, assuming the projects are comparable and the correct hurdle rate has been used.
options.note: The page states the rule with both conditions, which is why it goes on to argue that determining the hurdle rate is a critical part of appraisal rather than a mechanical input.

options.t: Prefer the project with the highest total accounting profit over its life.
options.note: Total accounting profit is one of the three candidate measures the week separates, and the one it says does not directly incorporate cash flow, timing or risk.

options.t: Prefer the project with the highest average return on assets.
options.note: Average ROA is the second candidate measure. The page keeps it in the comparison to show where it conflicts with NPV, not as the rule.

options.t: Prefer whichever project recovers its initial outlay soonest.
options.note: That is the payback test, and the week rejects it as a decision rule: payback does not measure value creation, and a project can repay its investment yet still have a negative NPV.

quiz.q: In the week’s hurdle-rate example, what does the row for 10% record?
quiz.hint: Two of the three rows name a winning project. The middle one does something else.

options.t: Project A, because lower discounting increases the relative value of its later cash flows.
options.note: That is the 7% row. At 10% the notes record no preference at all.

options.t: Indifferent — the notes record ‘Both product the same NPV’.
options.note: Quoted as the notes write it. The page draws the general point from it: different cash-flow patterns can have the same economic value at one discount rate.

options.t: Project B, because earlier cash flows become relatively more valuable.
options.note: That is the 14% row, where the higher rate has tipped the comparison toward the earlier cash flows.

options.t: Neither project, because both have a negative NPV at that rate.
options.note: A negative NPV appears only at 14%, and only for project A. At 10% the two are simply equal.

quiz.q: As the hurdle rate rises, what happens to a project that receives a greater proportion of its cash earlier?
quiz.hint: Think about which cash flows lose the most present value when the rate goes up.

options.t: It becomes relatively less attractive, because its cash has less time to grow at the higher rate.
options.note: That reasoning compounds forward. The appraisal discounts backward, and a higher rate punishes the flows that are furthest away.

options.t: Its NPV is unaffected, because only distant cash flows are exposed to the rate.
options.note: Every future flow is discounted; the difference is how heavily. Early flows retain more of their present value, they do not escape the rate.

options.t: It is preferred only if it also reports the higher accounting profit.
options.note: This reintroduces the measure the week is arguing against. NPV evaluates the actual cash-flow pattern rather than accounting profit.

options.t: It becomes relatively more attractive, because distant cash flows are discounted more heavily while early ones retain more of their present value.
options.note: The page gives exactly this chain, and the example follows it: project B, with more of its cash earlier, is preferred once the rate reaches 14%.

quiz.q: The week warns against automatically labelling a project superior. Which of these does it list as an inadequate basis for that label?
quiz.hint: One of the three items in that list is about NPV itself, which is what makes it worth remembering.

options.t: A higher NPV calculated using an inadequately justified discount rate.
options.note: The page lists it alongside higher total profits and higher accounting returns, and closes by saying a positive NPV is only as credible as the risk assessment underlying the hurdle rate.

options.t: A higher NPV calculated at a hurdle rate that reflects the project’s risk.
options.note: This is the case the week endorses rather than warns about — the rule is to prefer the highest positive NPV where the correct hurdle rate has been used.

options.t: An earlier cash-flow pattern, which the week says settles the ranking whatever the rate.
options.note: The week says the ranking is a joint property of the cash flows and the rate applied to them, so timing alone settles nothing.

options.t: A positive NPV supported by a documented assessment of the project’s risk.
options.note: That is what the page asks management to establish, not something it treats as an unsafe basis for a decision.

quiz.q: Which cash flows does Excel’s NPV() function discount, and what follows for the initial investment?
quiz.hint: The question is what has already happened by the time the function starts counting periods.

options.t: All the cash flows in the range including time 0, so the outlay simply goes in first.
options.note: This is the common error the page flags: including the time-0 investment inside the function would incorrectly discount a cash flow that already occurs today.

options.t: Future cash flows only, so the outlay should be discounted separately and then added.
options.note: Half right. The outlay occurs today, so there is nothing to discount — it is added at face value, outside the function.

options.t: Future cash flows only, so the time-0 investment must be added separately, where CF0 is normally negative.
options.note: Exactly what the page says. The function starts at period one, so anything already occurring today has to be brought in outside it.

options.t: Future cash flows only, so the outlay can be left out because it is already spent.
options.note: Leaving it out removes the initial outlay from NPV altogether, and NPV is the present value of the future cash flows less that outlay.

quiz.q: How does the week define the internal rate of return?
quiz.hint: The definition is a statement about one particular value that another measure takes.

options.t: The rate of return the providers of capital require, given the project’s risk.
options.note: That is the hurdle rate, and it is set outside the project. IRR is produced by the project’s own cash flows, and the two are then compared.

options.t: The discount rate that makes an investment’s NPV equal to zero.
options.note: The page states it as NPV = 0 at r = IRR, and calls it the investment’s implied annual return, set by the cash flows generated and the timing of those cash flows.

options.t: The average accounting return the investment earns on the assets it ties up.
options.note: That describes average ROA, which the week separates from IRR on exactly this point: ROA is built from profit and asset values, IRR from cash flows.

options.t: The rate at which the dollar value created by the investment grows each year.
options.note: The week reads it forward as the rate at which the investment itself is effectively growing as its cash flows occur and compound. Dollar value created is what NPV reports, and IRR does not measure it directly.

quiz.q: The week sets IRR against accounting ROA and NPV. On its own table, which measure reports the amount of economic value created?
quiz.hint: Two of the three measures recognise when the cash arrives. Only one of them is denominated in dollars.

options.t: Accounting ROA, because it is measured against the asset base the investment uses.
options.note: The table puts accounting ROA on profit and asset values, records that it does not recognise timing, and interprets it as accounting profitability rather than value created.

options.t: IRR, because it is built from the project’s cash flows rather than its profit.
options.note: Being cash-based and timing-aware is how IRR improves on accounting return, but the page is explicit that it does not directly measure the amount of economic value created.

options.t: All three, since the week treats them as three routes to the same answer.
options.note: The whole point of the table is that they differ in what they are built from and in whether they recognise when the money arrives, which is why they can rank projects differently.

options.t: NPV, because it discounts the cash flows at the required return and reports dollar value created.
options.note: That is the table’s third row exactly, and it is why the week says IRR answers ‘what percentage return does this investment generate?’ while NPV answers ‘how much value does it create?’

quiz.q: Project A has an IRR of 13.8% and Project B an IRR of 14.6%, and the two are mutually exclusive. What does the week conclude from this pair?
quiz.hint: Ask whether the NPV comparison of the same two projects gives one answer or several.

options.t: The project with the highest IRR does not necessarily have the highest NPV.
options.note: IRR alone ranks B above A on the two percentages, while NPV prefers A at some hurdle rates and B at others, with the two equal at 10%. The comparison of percentages and the comparison of present values do not have to agree.

options.t: Project B should be selected, because a higher IRR means a higher NPV at every hurdle rate.
options.note: This is the inference the section exists to block. At 10% the two projects have equal NPVs, and at other rates the preference moves either way.

options.t: Neither project should proceed, because both IRRs sit below the hurdle rate.
options.note: The week does not set either IRR against a fixed hurdle rate here. Its point is about the order the two measures put the projects in, not about whether they clear a threshold.

options.t: The IRRs are too close together to separate the projects, so accounting profit should decide.
options.note: The week never falls back on accounting profit — it argues throughout that profit does not directly incorporate cash flow, timing or risk. Where IRR and NPV conflict, it says prefer NPV.

quiz.q: Excel calculates IRR from a project’s cash flows. Which cash flows does the week say go into it?
quiz.hint: Compare it with what the same week says about handing cash flows to the NPV() function.

options.t: The future cash flows only, with the time-0 outlay added separately afterwards.
options.note: That is the handling the week prescribes for Excel’s NPV() function, where the initial investment occurs at time 0 and must be added separately, with CF0 normally negative. The IRR calculation is described differently.

options.t: Only the cash flows that arrive after the initial outlay has been recovered.
options.note: Recovering the outlay is what payback measures, and the week treats payback as a separate measure with its own problems. It plays no part in how IRR is calculated.

options.t: All project cash flows, including the initial time-0 outlay.
options.note: The page states it plainly and writes the entry as ‘=IFR(CF0:CFn)’, exactly as my notes write it. The series goes in whole, time-0 outlay included, and the rate comes back out.

options.t: The cash flows after each has been discounted at the hurdle rate.
options.note: That would presuppose the rate the calculation is meant to find. IRR is the rate at which NPV equals zero, so it is solved for rather than supplied.

quiz.q: What role does the week say IRR should play in a choice between mutually exclusive investments?
quiz.hint: The week is happy with IRR somewhere else entirely, and the contrast is the answer.

options.t: The primary criterion, because a percentage return is easy to communicate and compare with a hurdle rate.
options.note: The week grants that this is why IRR is popular, then says its interaction and underlying mathematics can create problems when comparing alternative projects.

options.t: A tie-breaker, used only when two projects report the same NPV.
options.note: The page assigns it no such job. It gives IRR a standing role as a support to the decision, and reserves the ranking itself for NPV.

options.t: No role at all, since a cash-flow-based measure is redundant once NPV is available.
options.note: The week keeps IRR in the toolkit — it is most useful for standalone investment assessment, where management wants an intuitive percentage return.

options.t: A supporting appraisal measure rather than the primary value creation criterion.
options.note: The page says exactly this, adds that a higher IRR does not automatically make a mutually exclusive investment economically superior, and tells managers to ask whether an attractive IRR also corresponds to the highest value creation at the relevant hurdle rate.

quiz.q: The week tests every appraisal method against three criteria — cash flow, timing of cash flow and risk. Why does it say NPV satisfies all three?
quiz.hint: Two of the criteria are in what NPV takes as its input; the third is in the rate it applies to them.

options.t: Because it is calculated from audited accounting figures rather than forecasts.
options.note: NPV is built from the project’s actual cash-flow pattern rather than accounting profit, so it is forecast cash flows it works from, not audited accounting figures.

options.t: Because it discounts future cash flows at a hurdle rate reflecting risk.
options.note: The page states it in one line. Cash flows supply the first criterion, discounting them by when they arrive supplies the second, and the hurdle rate carries the risk.

options.t: Because it averages the return over the whole life of the investment.
options.note: Averaging is the weakness the week attaches to average accounting ROA — it removes information about when returns occur, and the notes add that averaging is particularly problematic in finance because timing matters.

options.t: Because it expresses the answer as a percentage that can be compared with the required return.
options.note: That is IRR’s appeal, not NPV’s. NPV measures value creation in dollar terms, and the week warns that percentage returns should not be confused with dollar value creation.

quiz.q: The week reproduces its payback table as written, noting that the first row records a strength rather than a problem. Which row is it?
quiz.hint: Three of the four rows say what payback leaves out. One says what it manages to pick up.

options.t: Recognises cash flow — a useful starting point.
options.note: That is the row, and the page flags it in advance: the table is headed as payback’s problems, but the first entry is a strength and is reproduced here as written.

options.t: Ignores timing within the payback period.
options.note: A genuine problem, and the one the two-project example is built to demonstrate: payback treats early and late cash flows as equivalent.

options.t: Ignores risk.
options.note: Also a problem — because it ignores risk, payback cannot distinguish investments with different uncertainty.

options.t: Does not measure value creation.
options.note: The most serious of the problems: a project can repay its investment yet still have a negative NPV.

quiz.q: Project A invests 100 and receives 50, then 50; Project B invests 100 and receives 90, then 10. What does the week draw from the pair?
quiz.hint: Start by working out what payback says about each, then look at what the discounted figures say.

options.t: A is preferred, because spreading the recovery evenly reduces the risk of the investment.
options.note: The page ranks them the other way and on value, not on an even profile. It also says payback ignores risk altogether, so it cannot support a risk argument.

options.t: The two are equivalent investments, since both recover the outlay over the same span.
options.note: This is the inference the example is built to break. Its stated implication is that equal payback periods do not imply equal investments.

options.t: Both have a 2-year-payback, yet B is more valuable because more cash arrives earlier.
options.note: The page’s own wording. At 10% A’s PV is 86.8, giving NPV = -13.2, and B’s is 90.1, giving NPV = -9.9 — so both recover their nominal investment but still destroy economic value.

options.t: B is the better project because its positive NPV clears the hurdle rate while A’s does not.
options.note: Neither NPV is positive here — the values quoted are -9.9 and -13.2. B is the less bad of two value-destroying projects, which is precisely why payback is unsafe as a decision rule.

quiz.q: Beyond resting on accounting profit, what does the week say the act of averaging itself does to a return measure?
quiz.hint: Ask what a single average figure can no longer tell you about a sequence of returns.

options.t: It overstates the return, because early years carry the same weight as later ones.
options.note: The page makes no claim about the direction of the error. Its objection is to the information the average discards, not to a bias in the number.

options.t: It makes the measure sensitive to the hurdle rate chosen.
options.note: The reverse: average ROA does not explicitly incorporate risk, and the week’s complaint is that no hurdle rate enters it at all.

options.t: It converts a percentage return into a dollar figure that cannot be compared across projects.
options.note: Average ROA stays an accounting return. Confusing percentage returns with dollar value creation is the warning the week attaches to IRR.

options.t: It removes information about when returns occur, and averaging is particularly problematic in finance because timing matters.
options.note: The second of the three grounds the week gives, alongside using accounting profit rather than cash flow and not explicitly incorporating risk. Average ROA may describe accounting performance, but it should not determine which investment creates the most value.

quiz.q: What reinvestment assumption does the week say is commonly attributed to IRR, and when does it become hardest to accept?
quiz.hint: The assumption is about what happens to the cash that comes back before the project ends.

options.t: That interim cash flows are reinvested at the hurdle rate, which is unrealistic when the hurdle rate is low.
options.note: The rate in the assumption is the project’s own IRR, not the hurdle rate — which is exactly why a very high IRR makes it hard to believe.

options.t: That interim cash flows are reinvested at the project’s IRR, which may be unrealistic where the calculated IRR is very high.
options.note: The page’s wording, given as an interpretation commonly placed on IRR rather than as a mechanical property. The higher the IRR, the stronger the claim about what can be done with the money coming back.

options.t: That interim cash flows are held as cash until the project ends, which understates the return.
options.note: The week describes the opposite assumption — that the money is put back to work, and at an ambitious rate.

options.t: That interim cash flows are reinvested in the same project, which is impossible for a mutually exclusive investment.
options.note: The assumption concerns the rate the cash earns, not where it goes. Mutual exclusivity is a separate problem, and the week raises it under ranking conflict and scale.

quiz.q: Investment X has an outlay of 20m and a year 1 cash flow of 40m, an IRR of 100% and an NPV at 10% of 16.4m. Investment Y has an outlay of 40m and a year 1 cash flow of 70m, an IRR of 75% and an NPV at 10% of 23.6m. What does this pair illustrate?
quiz.hint: Look at which measure puts X first and which puts Y first, then at what separates the two investments.

options.t: The reinvestment assumption, because X’s very high IRR could not realistically be earned on the cash it returns.
options.note: The reinvestment assumption is a separate problem the week raises just before this table. Here the two measures are being applied to the same two projects and disagree on the order.

options.t: The timing problem, because Y’s cash arrives later than X’s.
options.note: Both cash flows land in year 1, so timing is not what separates them. IRR does incorporate the timing of cash flow — it is one of the two criteria the week credits it with.

options.t: The scale problem — IRR ranks X first because 100% > 75%, while NPV ranks Y first because it creates more economic value.
options.note: The week’s own reading of the table. IRR measures a percentage return, so it can favour a smaller project with a high growth rate even when a larger project creates more dollar value, and it ignores the size of the investment base when comparing projects.

options.t: That a project can repay its outlay and still destroy value, since both recover their investment within the year.
options.note: That is the payback lesson, drawn from the two projects with equal payback and negative NPVs. Both X and Y have positive NPVs at 10%; the question is only which of them creates more value.

scenarios.title: The offer that pays next year
scenarios.setup: A supplier offers your team an arrangement that requires capital now and returns a single cash amount in twelve months. A colleague looks at the two numbers, sees that the amount coming back is larger than the amount going out, and calls it a clear win. Your finance lead is unconvinced and asks for the case in today’s dollars.
scenarios.task: Explain why the future amount cannot be set against today’s outlay as it stands, and show — using the week’s own worked example — how much value the investment actually creates.
hints: The comparison your colleague is making has two numbers standing at two different points in time.
Before anything counts as value created, the capital has to earn what its providers require.
The week is deliberate that the surplus in future dollars and the value created today are two different figures.
walkthrough: Start with the benchmark rather than the outlay. If $100,000 of capital costs 10%, it must grow to $110,000 after one year simply to satisfy the required return, so $110,000 — not $100,000 — is what the investment has to beat.
Compare the cash generated with that benchmark. The investment produces $112,000, so the excess is $2000, and the week is careful to label this as value created in future-dollar terms.
Discount the surplus. $2000/1.10 = $1818, so the investment creates $1818 of value today. The future surplus and today’s value creation are not the same amount.
Reach the same answer through NPV. Restating the future cash flow in today’s terms gives NPV = $101818 - $100000 = $1818 — the outlay is never compared directly with the nominal future cash flow.

Answer the week’s framing question: are the expected future cash flows worth more today than the capital required to obtain them? Here they are, by $1818, and that dollar figure is the measure of the economic value generated.
checklist: Names the required return, not the initial outlay, as the benchmark the cash has to clear.
Keeps the future-dollar surplus and today’s value creation distinct, and says why the distinction matters.
Expresses the future cash flow in today’s terms before subtracting the outlay.
States the conclusion as a dollar amount of value created, not just as a positive or negative verdict.

scenarios.title: The platform that reports a loss
scenarios.setup: A capital-intensive platform your organisation built two years ago carries a heavy depreciation charge and has reported an accounting loss in every year since launch. At the quarterly review a board member points at the loss line and proposes shutting it down. Nobody in the room has yet mentioned the cash the platform generates.
scenarios.task: Decide what you would need to establish before you could accept that the reported loss shows the platform is destroying value.
hints: Ask what actually left the bank account when that depreciation charge was recorded.
The week gives a one-line relationship that turns a reported profit figure into the cash the project generated.
Even once you have the cash figure, the week says profit misses three things — and cash alone is only the first of them.
walkthrough: Separate the charge from the cash. Depreciation is an accounting expense but not a current cash outflow, so the loss is reported after a charge that no money left the business to pay.

Recover the cash figure. Cash Flow = Profit + Depreciation, where depreciation is the relevant non-cash expense and taxes are excluded. A project can report an accounting loss while still generating positive cash flow.

Say why that is the figure that matters here. For investment valuation the relevant measure is the cash generated, because value ultimately depends on the cash available to investors rather than on accounting earnings.

Do not stop at cash. Accounting profit does not directly incorporate cash flow + timing of cash flow + risk, so the appraisal still needs the timing of those cash flows and a hurdle rate that reflects the platform’s risk.

Frame the recommendation as the week does: ranking on profit alone can produce a different answer from ranking on economic value, so the loss line is a prompt to run the appraisal, not a decision in itself.
checklist: Identifies depreciation as the reason profit and cash diverge, and states that no cash left the business for it.
Uses the week’s relationship to move from the reported profit to cash flow, noting that taxes are excluded.
Explains why cash generated is the relevant measure for valuation.
Refuses to settle the decision on cash alone, and names timing and risk as still outstanding.

scenarios.title: Two bids, one discount rate
scenarios.setup: Two vendors have bid for the same replacement system and the bids are mutually exclusive — choosing one rejects the other. Both deliver the same service outcome, but one returns a greater proportion of its benefits in the early years while the other builds more slowly toward larger later savings. The appraisal was signed off at one hurdle rate, and the risk committee now argues that rate was set too low for a project of this kind.
scenarios.task: Work out how raising the hurdle rate could change which bid is preferred, and what that means for the recommendation already on the table.
hints: The ranking is not a property of the bids alone.
A higher rate does not treat the two bids’ cash flows evenly — think about which flows lose the most.
The week works an example in which the preferred project changes twice as the rate moves, and one of the rates produces no preference at all.
walkthrough: State what the hurdle rate is. The Hurdle Rate / WACC / cost of capital represents the minimum return given the project’s risk: higher perceived risk → higher hurdle rate, lower perceived risk → lower hurdle rate.

Trace the effect on the two profiles. As the rate rises, distant cash flows are discounted more heavily while early cash flows retain more of their present value, so the bid that generates cash sooner becomes relatively more attractive.

Read the week’s example as the pattern. At 7% project A is preferred because lower discounting increases the relative value of its later cash flows; at 10% the notes record indifference — ‘Both product the same NPV’; at 14% project B is preferred, and project A has a negative NPV, meaning it fails to earn the required return and destroys value.

Apply the general lesson. NPV is not simply a property of the project’s cash flows; it also depends on the required rate of return applied to them, so two projects can switch rankings when the hurdle rate changes because their cash-flow timing differs.

Conclude on the recommendation. The signed-off ranking cannot be defended until the rate behind it is defended, since determining the appropriate hurdle rate is a critical part of investment appraisal, not merely a mechanical input.
checklist: Links the hurdle rate to the project’s risk in both directions.
Explains the mechanism — heavier discounting of distant flows — rather than only asserting that the ranking moves.
Recognises that a rate exists at which the two are equal, and that a bid can turn value-destroying at a higher rate.
Treats the choice of rate as part of the appraisal to be justified, not an assumption inherited from the paper.

scenarios.title: Three measures, one recommendation
scenarios.setup: A paper comes to you recommending one of two mutually exclusive proposals. It ranks them on total accounting profit and on average return on assets, and the same proposal wins on both. There is an NPV in an appendix, calculated in a spreadsheet, and the discount rate used is stated once with no supporting reasoning.
scenarios.task: Assess how much confidence the paper’s recommendation deserves, and set out what you would ask for before signing it.
hints: The paper leads with two of the three measures the week separates. Ask what those two leave out.
Two measures agreeing does not make them independent evidence if they share the same blind spot.
The week has a specific warning about a spreadsheet NPV, and a second about a rate nobody has justified.
walkthrough: Sort the measures. The week separates three: total accounting profit, average return on assets, and NPV. The paper leads with the first two.

Name the shared weakness. Total accounting profit does not directly incorporate cash flow, timing of cash flow or risk, and average ROA remains an accounting-based measure that does not fully incorporate cash-flow timing or risk — so the two agreeing tells you little, and average ROA can favour higher accounting profits even where the other proposal generates cash earlier.

Move the comparison onto cash. NPV evaluates projects using their actual cash-flow pattern rather than accounting profit, and for mutually exclusive projects the rule is to prefer the highest positive NPV, assuming the projects are comparable and the correct hurdle rate has been used.

Audit the spreadsheet before trusting the appendix figure. Excel’s NPV() function discounts future cash flows only, so the time-0 investment must be added separately, where CF0 is normally negative; including it inside the function would incorrectly discount a cash flow that already occurs today.

Test the rate. A project should not be labelled superior on higher total profits, on higher accounting returns, or on a higher NPV calculated using an inadequately justified discount rate — a positive NPV is only as credible as the risk assessment underlying the hurdle rate.
Return the paper with the week’s two questions attached: are the cash-flow forecasts credible, and is the discount rate appropriate for their risk?
checklist: Distinguishes the three measures and says what each one does and does not take into account.
Explains why agreement between profit and average ROA is weak evidence rather than confirmation.
Checks the mechanics of the spreadsheet NPV, including how the time-0 outlay is handled.
Challenges the discount rate as part of the appraisal, and ties the NPV’s credibility to the risk assessment behind it.
Ends with a decision framed around greatest value after cash flow, timing and risk — not highest reported profit.

scenarios.title: The bid with the higher IRR
scenarios.setup: Two mutually exclusive proposals for the same digital platform reach the investment committee. The sponsor’s slide leads with a single line for each: one returns 13.8%, the other 14.6%. The committee is comfortable with percentages, has approved projects on that basis before, and is ready to take the higher of the two. An NPV analysis exists but is not on the slide.
scenarios.task: Decide whether the percentage on the slide is enough to settle the choice, and say what you would put in front of the committee instead.
hints: Ask what question the number on the slide is answering, and whether it is the question the committee is being asked.
The two proposals rule each other out, and the week treats that case differently from a single investment assessed on its own.
A ranking by IRR gives one fixed answer. Check whether the other measure of the same two projects behaves the same way.
walkthrough: Say what the number is. IRR is the discount rate that makes an investment’s NPV equal to zero — NPV = 0 at r = IRR — so it reports the investment’s implied annual return, set by the cash flows generated and their timing.
Give it its due. IRR improves on accounting return by incorporating cash and timing, and a percentage is easy to communicate and to compare with a hurdle rate. That is why the committee likes it.

Name the limit. IRR does not directly measure the amount of economic value created — that is what NPV reports — and the week’s own pair of projects, at 13.8% and 14.6%, shows that the project with the highest IRR does not necessarily have the highest NPV.

Show how the two measures behave differently here. Ranking by IRR gives one fixed answer, while NPV prefers one project at some hurdle rates and the other at different rates, with the two equal at 10%. Different cash-flow patterns can cause IRR and NPV to produce conflicting rankings.

Put the resolution rule on the slide. When IRR and NPV conflict, prefer NPV; IRR belongs here as a supporting appraisal measure rather than the primary value creation criterion, and is at its most useful for a standalone investment assessed against the hurdle rate.
Close with the question the week gives managers: does the attractive IRR also correspond to the highest value creation at the relevant hurdle rate?
checklist: Defines IRR as the rate at which NPV is zero, rather than as a return on capital employed.
Credits IRR with cash and timing before criticising it, so the argument is not that the measure is worthless.
Distinguishes standalone assessment, where the week endorses IRR, from a mutually exclusive choice, where it does not.
States the conflict rule explicitly and asks for the dollar value created at the relevant hurdle rate.

scenarios.title: The two-year payback rule
scenarios.setup: A division applies a standing rule that any technology investment must repay its initial cost within two years. Two proposals arrive that both clear it exactly: each recovers its outlay over two years, so on the rule they are interchangeable, and the division head proposes picking on delivery convenience. Neither proposal has been discounted.
scenarios.task: Decide whether the payback rule has actually told the division anything about which proposal to take, and what it has failed to tell them.
hints: Payback is not worthless — start with the one thing the week’s table credits it with.
Two projects can reach the same recovery point along very different paths.
Clearing the rule and creating value are separate questions, and the week has an example where a project does the first without the second.
walkthrough: Say what payback measures: how long it takes to recover the initial investment from future cash inflows. It is popular because it is quick and easy to calculate, and the first row of the week’s table records a genuine strength — it recognises cash flow, which makes it a useful starting point.

Then take the table’s remaining rows in turn. Payback ignores timing within the payback period, so it treats early and late cash flows as equivalent; it ignores risk, so it cannot distinguish investments with different uncertainty; and it does not measure value creation, so a project can repay its investment yet still have negative NPV.

Work the week’s example. Project A invests 100 and receives 50, then 50; Project B invests 100 and receives 90, then 10. Both have a 2-year-payback, yet B is more valuable because more cash arrives earlier.

Discount them. At 10%, A’s present value is 86.8 giving NPV = -13.2, and B’s is 90.1 giving NPV = -9.9. Both recover their nominal investment but still destroy economic value — so the rule has cleared two projects that a value test rejects.
State the implication as the week does: equal payback periods do not imply equal investments. The rule has ranked nothing and has certified nothing.

Recommend the test the week prefers. NPV uses actual cash flows, recognises when those cash flows occur, incorporates risk through the hurdle rate and measures value creation in dollar terms, so run both proposals through it at an appropriately estimated hurdle rate before choosing.
checklist: Credits payback with recognising cash flow before setting out what it leaves out.
Separates ignoring timing, ignoring risk and not measuring value creation as three distinct failures.
Uses the week’s figures to show two projects with identical payback and different values, and notes that both NPVs are negative.
Concludes that clearing a payback threshold is not evidence of value creation.
Recommends NPV at a justified hurdle rate as the replacement test.

scenarios.title: The small project with the big percentage
scenarios.setup: Two investments compete for the same approval. Investment X has an outlay of 20m and a year 1 cash flow of 40m, an IRR of 100% and an NPV at 10% of 16.4m. Investment Y has an outlay of 40m and a year 1 cash flow of 70m, an IRR of 75% and an NPV at 10% of 23.6m. The papers have been ranked on IRR and X is at the top of the list.
scenarios.task: Work out which investment the week would have the committee approve, and explain why the ranking on the papers came out the other way.
hints: Both cash flows arrive in year 1, so whatever is separating these two, it is not timing.
Look at what changes between the two investments other than the return each earns.
One measure is denominated in a percentage and one in dollars, and the week is insistent that they are not the same claim.
walkthrough: Establish what IRR does capture, so the criticism is targeted. It incorporates cash flow and the timing of cash flow, but it does not incorporate project risk on its own, which is why the IRR must be compared against an independently estimated hurdle rate.
Read the two rankings off the figures. IRR ranks X first because 100% > 75%; NPV ranks Y first because it creates more economic value — 23.6m against 16.4m at a 10% rate.

Name the cause. This is the scale problem: IRR measures a percentage return, so it can favour a smaller project with a high growth rate even when a larger project creates more dollar value. IRR ignores the size of the investment base when comparing projects.

Rule out the other explanations. Both flows land in year 1, so timing is not doing the work, and the reinvestment assumption — that interim cash flows are reinvested at the project’s IRR — is a separate objection the week raises alongside this one.
Apply the decision rule. For mutually exclusive projects, choose the investment with the highest positive NPV, using an appropriately estimated hurdle rate — so Y, on these figures at 10%.

Generalise it the way the week closes: a quick or intuitive appraisal measure is not necessarily a good decision rule, percentage returns should not be confused with dollar value creation, and where common appraisals measure conflict, rely on NPV.
checklist: States what IRR incorporates before setting out what it misses, and notes that risk has to come from a separately estimated hurdle rate.
Reads both rankings off the figures rather than asserting the conflict.
Identifies scale — the size of the investment base — as what separates the two, and rules timing out.
Selects on the highest positive NPV at an appropriately estimated hurdle rate.
Ends on the distinction between a percentage return and dollar value creation.
